claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation is an essential post-translational modification in metazoans despite its low abundance relative to serine and threonine phosphorylation.
source: Despite its low abundance relative to serine and threonine phosphorylation, tyrosine phosphorylation is an essential post-translational modification in metazoans (Lim and Pawson, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lim and Pawson, 2010

claim: Tyrosine kinases and SH2 domains must have the ability to discriminate among a myriad of potential phosphorylation sites in the proteome to ensure proper signal transduction.
source: Tyrosine kinases, the enzymes that phosphorylate tyrosine residues on proteins, and Src homology 2 (SH2) domains, protein modules that bind tyrosine-phosphorylated sequences, must have the ability to discriminate among a myriad of potential phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in the proteome, in order to ensure proper signal transduction.
evidence: Based on established understanding of signal transduction specificity

claim: The preferential engagement of specific phosphosites by tyrosine kinases and SH2 domains is dependent on the amino acid sequence surrounding the tyrosine or phosphotyrosine residue.
source: The preferential engagement of specific phosphosites by tyrosine kinases and SH2 domains is dependent on the amino acid sequence surrounding the tyrosine or phosphotyrosine residue (Songyang et al., 1995; Songyang et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995 and 1993

claim: Isolated tyrosine kinase domains most efficiently engage phosphosites that conform to specific sequence motifs defined by a small number of key residues.
source: Isolated tyrosine kinase domains most efficiently engage phosphosites that conform to specific sequence motifs, which are defined by a small number of key residues that contribute significantly to recognition (Songyang et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Songyang et al., 1995

claim: Negative selection of specific sequence features can play a role in kinase specificity.
source: Negative selection of specific sequence features can also play a role in kinase specificity (Alexander et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alexander et al., 2011

claim: The T cell tyrosine kinase ZAP-70 cannot readily phosphorylate co-localized proteins that contain even a modest positive charge.
source: For example, the T cell tyrosine kinase ZAP-70 cannot readily phosphorylate co-localized proteins that contain even a modest positive charge (Shah et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shah et al., 2016

claim: Binding domains such as SH2 domains can strongly influence specificity by localizing kinases to the vicinity of phosphorylation targets.
source: Binding domains, such as SH2 domains, can strongly influence specificity by localizing kinases to the vicinity of phosphorylation targets (Pawson and Nash, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pawson and Nash, 2000

claim: Secondary interactions between SH2 and kinase domains can refine the substrate preferences of a tyrosine kinase by stabilizing its active state.
source: Secondary interactions between SH2 and kinase domains can also refine the substrate preferences of a tyrosine kinase by stabilizing its active state (Filippakopoulos et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Filippakopoulos et al., 2008

claim: The most prominent approach to characterize sequence recognition by tyrosine kinases and SH2 domains employs purified kinases/SH2 domains and oriented peptide libraries.
source: The most prominent approach employs purified kinases/SH2 domains and oriented peptide libraries, which are synthetic, degenerate peptide libraries with a central tyrosine or phosphotyrosine residue (Songyang et al., 1995; Songyang et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citations to Songyang et al., 1995 and 1993

claim: Large swaths of the yeast and human kinomes have been characterized using oriented peptide libraries.
source: Notably, this method is also applicable to serine/threonine kinases, and large swaths of the yeast and human kinomes have been characterized using oriented peptide libraries, providing significant insights into kinase-substrate recognition and phospho-signaling (Deng et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2023; Mok et al., 2010; Songyang et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Deng et al., 2014; Johnson et al., 2023; Mok et al., 2010; Songyang et al., 1995

claim: Some amino acid preferences may depend on the surrounding sequence context.
source: Oriented peptide library screens have primarily been useful for determining the preference for each amino acid at a given position, independent of sequence context, but evidence suggests that some amino acid preferences may depend on the surrounding sequence (Cantor et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cantor et al., 2018

claim: The X5-Y-X5 library contains 1-10 million unique peptide sequences.
source: Deep sequencing of both versions of the X5-Y-X5 library confirmed that they have 1–10 million unique peptide sequences, 20% of which contain one or more stop codons.
evidence: Confirmed by deep sequencing analysis

claim: 20% of sequences in the X5-Y-X5 library contain one or more stop codons.
source: Deep sequencing of both versions of the X5-Y-X5 library confirmed that they have 1–10 million unique peptide sequences, 20% of which contain one or more stop codons.
evidence: Confirmed by deep sequencing analysis

claim: All 20 canonical amino acids were well-represented at each of the 10 variable positions surrounding the fixed tyrosine residue in the X5-Y-X5 library.
source: Furthermore, all 20 canonical amino acids were well-represented at each of the 10 variable positions surrounding the fixed tyrosine residue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confirmed by deep sequencing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The position-specific amino acid preferences of c-Src determined from the X5-Y-X5 screen matched the sequence specificity defined by prior reports using oriented peptide libraries.
source: The preferences determined from this screen matched the sequence specificity of c-Src defined by prior reports using oriented peptide libraries (Deng et al., 2014; Songyang et al., 1995).
evidence: Comparison with previously published data from Deng et al., 2014 and Songyang et al., 1995

claim: c-Src shows a strong preference for bulky aliphatic residues (Ile/Leu/Val) at the -1 position relative to the central tyrosine.
source: We observed a strong preference for bulky aliphatic residues (Ile/Leu/Val) at the –1 position relative to the central tyrosine and a phenylalanine at the +3 position (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: c-Src shows a strong preference for phenylalanine at the +3 position relative to the central tyrosine.
source: We observed a strong preference for bulky aliphatic residues (Ile/Leu/Val) at the –1 position relative to the central tyrosine and a phenylalanine at the +3 position (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: c-Src shows a strong preference for +1 Asp/Glu/Ser in addition to the previously reported +1 Gly.
source: Our results showed modest differences from the specificity observed by oriented peptide libraries, including a strong preference for a+1 Asp/Glu/Ser in addition to the previously reported +1 Gly.
evidence: Observed in screening data, compared to previous literature

claim: The position-specific amino acid enrichments obtained using two different biotinylated pan-phosphotyrosine antibodies were nearly identical.
source: The position-specific amino acid enrichments obtained using both antibodies were nearly identical (Figure 1C).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 1C

claim: There is no significant bias in the enrichment of peptides introduced by the pan-phosphotyrosine antibody.
source: This suggests that there is no significant bias in the enrichment of peptides introduced by the pan-phosphotyrosine antibody.
evidence: Inferred from the nearly identical results with two different antibodies

claim: c-Abl prefers bulky aliphatic residues at the -1 position with respect to the central tyrosine.
source: Like c-Src, c-Abl preferred bulky aliphatic residues at the –1 position with respect to the central tyrosine.
evidence: Observed in screening data

claim: c-Abl prefers alanine at the +1 position.
source: Unlike c-Src, c-Abl preferred an alanine at the +1 position and had a notably strong preference for proline at the +3 position (Figures 1B and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figures 1B, 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: c-Abl has a notably strong preference for proline at the +3 position.
source: Unlike c-Src, c-Abl preferred an alanine at the +1 position and had a notably strong preference for proline at the +3 position (Figures 1B and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figures 1B, 2A, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Fer shows a preference for tryptophan residues at the +2, +3, and +4 positions.
source: Fer showed a specificity pattern distinct from both c-Src and c-Abl, which included a preference for tryptophan residues at the +2,+3, and +4 positions.
evidence: Observed in screening data

claim: EPHB1 and EPHB2 kinases have similar specificities.
source: As expected, the closely related EPHB1 and EPHB2 kinases had similar specificities, which included a unique preference for Asn and Asp at the –1 residue that was not observed for the tested non-receptor tyrosine kinases (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: EPHB1 and EPHB2 have a unique preference for Asn and Asp at the -1 residue that was not observed for the tested non-receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: As expected, the closely related EPHB1 and EPHB2 kinases had similar specificities, which included a unique preference for Asn and Asp at the –1 residue that was not observed for the tested non-receptor tyrosine kinases (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: The Src Consensus peptide had a higher maximal catalytic rate (kcat) but a lower apparent binding affinity (KM) when compared to both SrcTides.
source: Our Src Consensus peptide had a higher maximal catalytic rate (kcat) but a lower apparent binding affinity (KM) when compared to both SrcTides.
evidence: Measured using Michaelis-Menten analysis with the ADP-Quest assay, data shown in Table 1

claim: The Abl Consensus peptide had both a higher maximal rate (kcat) and tighter apparent affinity (KM) relative to the previously reported AblTide peptide.
source: For c-Abl, our consensus peptide had both a higher maximal rate (kcat) and tighter apparent affinity (KM) relative to the previously reported AblTide peptide (Table 1).
evidence: Measured using Michaelis-Menten analysis with the ADP-Quest assay, data shown in Table 1

claim: Different methods may be biased toward slightly different realms of sequence space for identifying high-efficiency substrates.
source: Collectively, these experiments suggest that different methods may be biased toward slightly different realms of sequence space, and that there are multiple solutions to achieving high-efficiency phosphorylation.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of consensus peptides with previously reported substrates

claim: For the non-receptor tyrosine kinases (c-Src, c-Abl, and Fer), the corresponding consensus peptides were the best substrates tested.
source: For the non-receptor tyrosine kinases (c-Src, c-Abl, and Fer), the corresponding consensus peptides were the best substrates tested.
evidence: Measured using in vitro kinetic assays, data shown in Figure 2C

claim: c-Abl efficiently phosphorylated the Src and EPHB2 consensus peptides at a higher substrate concentration (100 μM).
source: At a higher substrate concentration (100 μM), c-Abl also efficiently phosphorylated the Src and EPHB2 consensus peptides (Figure 2C), but selectivity for the Abl Consensus improved at a lower concentration (20 μM), consistent with selectivity being driven by KM for this set of peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Table 1).
evidence: Measured using in vitro kinetic assays, data shown in Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2, and Table 1

claim: c-Src was selective for the Src Consensus peptide at high concentrations (100 μM).
source: By contrast, c-Src was selective for the Src Consensus peptide at high concentrations (Figure 2C), but showed significant off-target activity toward the Fer Consensus at low concentrations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Measured using in vitro kinetic assays, data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: The Fer Consensus peptide has a remarkably tight KM for c-Src, with a low kcat as a trade-off.
source: Michaelis-Menten analysis of the Fer Consensus with c-Src revealed that it has a remarkably tight KM for c-Src, with a low kcat as a trade-off (Table 1).
evidence: Measured using Michaelis-Menten analysis, data shown in Table 1

claim: EPHB1 showed very little selectivity across the consensus peptides and did not prefer its own cognate consensus sequence.
source: Finally, we observed that the receptor tyrosine kinase EPHB1 showed very little selectivity across the consensus peptides and did not prefer its own cognate consensus sequence (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Measured using in vitro kinetic assays, data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: EPHB2 efficiently phosphorylated its own consensus peptide, as well as the Abl Consensus.
source: EPHB2, on the other hand, efficiently phosphorylated its own consensus peptide, as well as the Abl Consensus.
evidence: Measured using in vitro kinetic assays, data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Not all consensus peptides will be selective for their given kinase, as there can be overlap in substrate specificities.
source: These experiments demonstrate the applicability of our bacterial peptide display method to the design of high-activity substrates. Our results also suggest that not all consensus peptides will be selective for their given kinase, as there can be overlap in substrate specificities.
evidence: Inferred from kinetic data showing cross-reactivity

claim: The X5-Y-X5 screening data for c-Src correlated moderately well with the log-transformed rates of phosphorylation measured using an RP-HPLC assay.
source: We found that our predictions, which were derived from log-transformed enrichment scores, correlated moderately well with the log-transformed rates of phosphorylation by c-Src (Figure 3A).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The X5-Y-X5 screening data could accurately predict the directionality of the effects of five out of six mutations.
source: Focusing specifically on the effects of the mutations in this set of peptides, we found that the X5-Y-X5 screening data could accurately predict the directionality of the effects of five out of six mutations (Figure 3B).
evidence: Comparison of predicted and measured mutational effects shown in Figure 3B

claim: The pTyr-Var library is composed of 11-residue sequences spanning 3159 human phosphosites and 4760 disease-associated variants of these phosphosites bearing a single amino acid substitution.
source: To refine our assessment of phosphosite-proximal mutational effects, we designed a library, derived from the PhosphoSitePlus database, that is composed of 11-residue sequences spanning 3159 human phosphosites and 4760 disease-associated variants of these phosphosites bearing a single amino acid substitution (pTyr-Var library; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Hornbeck et al., 2019).
evidence: Library design described in text and Figure 4—figure supplement 1, based on PhosphoSitePlus database

claim: The pTyr-Var library totaled ~10,000 unique sequences.
source: Including these tyrosine mutants and additional control sequences, such as previously designed consensus substrates, the library totaled ~10,000 unique sequences.
evidence: Library design described in text

claim: Three to five replicates of the pTyr-Var screen were conducted with each kinase, and the results were reproducible across replicates.
source: Three to five replicates of the pTyr-Var screen were conducted with each kinase, and the results were reproducible across replicates (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Reproducibility shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: There was a strong correlation between the pTyr-Var enrichment scores and phosphorylation rates for c-Src, particularly for high-activity sequences.
source: We found a strong correlation between the pTyr-Var enrichment scores and phosphorylation rates, particularly for high-activity sequences (Figure 4B).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: The effects of mutations in the pTyr-Var screens were consistent with those observed using the in vitro RP-HPLC assay with purified peptides.
source: Furthermore, the effects of mutations in the screens were consistent with those observed using the in vitro RP-HPLC assay with purified peptides (Figure 4C).
evidence: Comparison shown in Figure 4C

claim: For every kinase tested, the tyrosine-free sequences showed distinctly low enrichment scores, consistent with signal in these screens being driven by tyrosine phosphorylation of the surface-displayed peptides.
source: For every kinase tested, the tyrosine-free sequences showed distinctly low enrichment scores, consistent with signal in these screens being driven by tyrosine phosphorylation of the surface-displayed peptides (Figure 4A).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4A

claim: For each kinase, a subset of the library (between 7% and 10%) showed enrichment scores above the background level.
source: For each kinase, a subset of the library (between 7% and 10%) showed enrichment scores above this background level (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: There was strong correlation in specificity between kinases of the same family (the Src-family kinases c-Src/Fyn/Hck, and receptor pairs EPHB1/EPHB2 and FGFR1/FGFR3).
source: We found strong correlation in specificity between kinases of the same family (the Src-family kinases c-Src/Fyn/Hck, and receptor pairs EPHB1/EPHB2 and FGFR1/FGFR3).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: The specificity of Src-family kinases partly overlapped with the Ephrin receptors and MERTK.
source: We also observed that the specificity of Src-family kinases partly overlapped with the Ephrin receptors and MERTK.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: The specificity of AncSZ and Jak2 correlated with that of FGFRs.
source: The specificity of AncSZ and Jak2 correlated with that of FGFRs.
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: For c-Src, Fyn, and c-Abl, out of the sequences that overlapped between the pTyr-Var library and the curated list of kinase-substrate pairs, 30-40% showed efficient phosphorylation in the peptide-display screen.
source: For c-Src, Fyn, and c-Abl, out of the sequences that overlapped between our library and the curated list, 30–40% of the kinase-substrate pairs showed efficient phosphorylation in the peptide-display screen (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Comparison with PhosphoSitePlus database, data shown in Figure 4—source data 1

claim: For c-Src, 381 high-confidence mutations were identified from the pTyr-Var screen.
source: For c-Src, we identified 381 high-confidence mutations (Figure 4E).
evidence: Filtering and analysis of screening data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Kinases showed distinct patterns of mutational sensitivity at each position around the central tyrosine.
source: From this filtered list, we found that kinases showed distinct patterns of mutational sensitivity at each position around the central tyrosine, consistent with their distinct sequence preferences (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Analysis of screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7

claim: The RET R982C mutation significantly enhanced phosphorylation of Tyr 981 by c-Src.
source: For example, we found that the R982C mutation, proximal to Tyr 981 on the receptor tyrosine kinase RET, significantly enhanced phosphorylation by c-Src (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8

claim: The RET R982C mutation also enhanced Tyr 981 phosphorylation by several other kinases, most notably Fer.
source: The RET R982C mutation also enhanced Tyr 981 phosphorylation by several other kinases, most notably Fer (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8

claim: The reference peptide for SHP2 Tyr 62 was preferentially phosphorylated by receptor tyrosine kinases, such as FGFR1, over non-receptors such as c-Src and Fyn.
source: In our screens, the reference peptide for Tyr 62 was preferentially phosphorylated by receptor tyrosine kinases, such as FGFR1, over non-receptors such as c-Src and Fyn, and nearby mutations showed varied effects on Tyr 62 phosphorylation, depending on the kinase tested (Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9

claim: The SHP2 D61V mutation enhanced and D61N attenuated phosphorylation of Tyr 62 by Src-family kinases, but these mutations had little impact on recognition by FGFR1.
source: For example, D61V enhanced and D61N attenuated phosphorylation by Src-family kinases, but these mutations had little impact on recognition by FGFR1.
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9

claim: Phosphorylation measurements of wild-type, D61V, and D61N SHP2 by c-Src, Fyn, and FGFR1 using intact protein mass spectrometry recapitulated the relative phosphorylation efficiencies for the Tyr 62 reference peptides.
source: Our measurements recapitulated the relative phosphorylation efficiencies for the Tyr 62 reference peptides, with Fyn being the slowest, and FGFR1 being the fastest (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Measured using intact protein mass spectrometry, data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 9

claim: Both D61V and D61N dramatically enhanced phosphorylation of SHP2 by all three kinases (c-Src, Fyn, and FGFR1).
source: Both D61V and D61N dramatically enhanced phosphorylation by all three kinases, consistent with reports that mutations at this site dramatically alter SHP2 structure and probably also increase Tyr 62 accessibility (Keilhack et al., 2005).
evidence: Measured using intact protein mass spectrometry, data shown in Figure 4F; consistent with citation to Keilhack et al., 2005

claim: For c-Src and Fyn, but not FGFR1, D61V showed a stronger enhancement of SHP2 phosphorylation than D61N.
source: For c-Src and Fyn, but not FGFR1, D61V showed a stronger enhancement of phosphorylation than D61N, consistent with our peptide screens (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Measured using intact protein mass spectrometry, data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 9

claim: For peptides that showed significant enrichment in the pTyr-Var screens (enrichment >1), there was a modest correlation with the scores predicted using the X5-Y-X5 library, with many outliers.
source: For peptides that showed significant enrichment in the pTyr-Var screens (enrichment >1), there was a modest correlation with the scores predicted using the X5-Y-X5 library, with many outliers (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Phosphorylation rates for selected peptides deviated from what would be expected based on a position-specific scoring matrix.
source: Phosphorylation rates for these peptides deviated from what would be expected based on a position-specific scoring matrix (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Measured using RP-HPLC assay, data shown in Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—source data 1

claim: The putatively unfavorable sequence features in selected peptides were tolerated in their specific sequence contexts.
source: This suggests that the putatively unfavorable sequence features in these peptides were tolerated in their specific sequence contexts.
evidence: Inferred from deviation of measured rates from predictions

claim: While the directionality of the effect of most mutations could be predicted by the X5-Y-X5 screen, many mutations showed a significant effect where none was predicted, as well as mutations where the effect was the opposite of what was predicted.
source: While the directionality of the effect of most mutations could be predicted by the X5-Y-X5 screen, we observed many mutations that showed a significant effect where none was predicted, as well as mutations where the effect was the opposite of what was predicted (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Comparison of predicted and measured mutational effects shown in Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and Figure 5—source data 2

claim: The same amino acid substitution (-2 Ser to Pro) had different impacts on c-Src recognition, depending on the sequence context.
source: Measurements of these purified peptides by c-Src show that the same amino acid substitution had different impacts on c-Src recognition, depending on the sequence context (Figure 5D).
evidence: Measured using RP-HPLC assay, data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Depending on the kinase, 5-15% of all significant mutations in the pTyr-Var screen had the opposite effect of that predicted using the X5-Y-X5 library data.
source: Depending on the kinase, 5–15% of all significant mutations in the pTyr-Var screen had the opposite effect of that predicted using the X5-Y-X5 library data.
evidence: Analysis of screening data

claim: The X5-Y-X5 library screens with c-Src, SHP2-C, and Grb2 SH2 domains recapitulated known sequence preferences for each SH2 domain.
source: The X5-Y-X5 library screens recapitulated known sequences preferences for each SH2 domain.
evidence: Comparison with previously published data

claim: For c-Src SH2 domain, there was a distinctive preference for -2 His, +1 Asp/Glu, and +3 Ile.
source: For c-Src, there was a distinctive preference for –2 His,+1 Asp/Glu, and +3 Ile, as previously reported from oriented peptide libraries (Huang et al., 2008).
evidence: Observed in screening data, consistent with citation to Huang et al., 2008

claim: For Grb2 SH2 domain, a characteristic +2 Asn preference dominated the specificity profile.
source: For Grb2, a characteristic +2 Asn preference dominated the specificity profile (Gram et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2008; Kessels et al., 2002; Rahuel et al., 1996; Songyang et al., 1994).
evidence: Observed in screening data, consistent with citations to Gram et al., 1997; Huang et al., 2008; Kessels et al., 2002; Rahuel et al., 1996; Songyang et al., 1994

claim: The Grb2 screen reveals subtle amino acid preferences at other positions, which could tune the affinity for +2 Asn-containing sequences.
source: Notably, our Grb2 screen also reveals subtle amino acid preferences at other positions, which could tune the affinity for +2 Asn-containing sequences.
evidence: Observed in screening data

claim: The SHP2 C-SH2 domain shows a preference for β-branched amino acids (Thr/Val/Ile) at the -2 position, a small residue (Ala/Ser/Thr) at the +1 position, and strong preference for an aliphatic residue (Ile/Val/Leu) at the +3 position.
source: Our method indicates a preference for β-branched amino acids (Thr/Val/Ile) at the –2 position, a small residue (Ala/Ser/Thr) at the +1 position, and strong preference for an aliphatic residue (Ile/Val/Leu) at the +3 position.
evidence: Observed in screening data

claim: The replicates for each SH2 domain in the pTyr-Var screen were highly correlated, but datasets between SH2 domains had poor correlation, suggesting distinct ligand specificities.
source: The replicates for each SH2 domain were highly correlated, but datasets between SH2 domains had poor correlation, suggesting distinct ligand specificities (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4

claim: Each SH2 domain showed strong enrichment of a few hundred peptides containing one or more tyrosines in the pTyr-Var screen.
source: As observed for kinases, we saw negligible enrichment of peptides lacking a tyrosine residue, but each SH2 domain showed strong enrichment of a few hundred peptides containing one or more tyrosines (Figure 6C).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Selection with the pan-phosphotyrosine antibody yielded a narrower distribution of enrichment scores compared to selection with SH2 domains, suggesting relatively uniform phosphorylation.
source: Compared to selection with SH2 domains, selection with the antibody yielded a narrower distribution of enrichment scores, with very few highly enriched sequences, suggesting relatively uniform phosphorylation (Figure 6C).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 6C

claim: Enrichment scores from the pTyr-Var screen with c-Src SH2 domain showed a good linear correlation with measured Kd values over two orders of magnitude.
source: Enrichment scores from the pTyr-Var screen showed a good linear correlation with measured Kd values over two orders of magnitude (Figure 6D).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 6D, comparing screening data with fluorescence polarization binding assay measurements

claim: For each SH2 domain, 50-300 phosphosite-proximal mutations were identified that significantly and reproducibly enhanced or attenuated binding.
source: For each SH2 domain, we identified 50–300 phosphosite-proximal mutations that significantly and reproducibly enhanced or attenuated binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Filtering and analysis of screening data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5 and Figure 6—source data 2

claim: The c-Src, SHP2-C, and Grb2 SH2 domains showed unique sensitivities to mutations.
source: As expected, given their distinct specificities, the c-Src, SHP2-C, and Grb2 SH2 domains showed unique sensitivities to mutations (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Analysis of screening data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6

claim: The phosphorylation profiles of c-Src kinase and SH2 domains against the pTyr-Var library were completely orthogonal.
source: Our screens revealed that the phosphorylation profiles of c-Src kinase and SH2 domains against the pTyr-Var were completely orthogonal (Figure 6—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Comparison of screening data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 7

claim: The starkly different activities of c-Src kinase and SH2 domains toward the pTyr-Var library can largely be attributed to kinase domain preference for a +3 Phe and SH2 domain preference for a +3 Ile/Val/Leu/Met.
source: Their starkly different activities toward the pTyr-Var library can largely be attributed to kinase domain preference for a+3 Phe and SH2 domain preference for a+3 Ile/Val/Leu/Met.
evidence: Analysis of screening data

claim: For c-Src, phosphosite mutations that impacted recognition by one domain generally had no effect on the other, because preferred sequence features for one domain were typically tolerated (neutral) for the other.
source: For c-Src, phosphosite mutations that impacted recognition by one domain generally had no effect on the other, because preferred sequence features for one domain were typically tolerated (neutral) for the other (Figure 6—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Analysis of screening data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 8

claim: Amber suppression with CMF or AzF was successfully achieved in the X5-Y-X5 library.
source: To confirm that non-canonical amino acids could be incorporated into the X5-Y-X5 library, we co-transformed E. coli with the library and a pULTRA-Amp plasmid encoding a tRNA/synthetase pair that can incorporate 4-carboxymethyl phenylalanine (CMF) via Amber suppression (Figure 7A; Xie et al., 2007).
evidence: Confirmed by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7B and 7C

claim: In the presence of CMF, premature termination at Amber codons was significantly suppressed.
source: In the presence of CMF, this premature termination was significantly suppressed, and a larger fraction of the cells displayed peptides.
evidence: Observed by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7B

claim: Only cells expressing the synthetase and grown in the presence of AzF showed significant DIBO labeling.
source: Only cells expressing the synthetase and grown in the presence of AzF showed significant DIBO labeling, confirming Amber suppression and non-canonical amino acid incorporation into our library (Figure 7C).
evidence: Observed by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 7C

claim: CMF was enriched at the -3 and -2 positions for c-Src, where Phe is not tolerated.
source: CMF was enriched at the –3 and –2 positions, where Phe is not tolerated by c-Src (Figure 7D).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 7D

claim: The negative charge on the carboxymethyl group of CMF at neutral pH may be able to mimic the recognition of negatively-charged amino acids (Asp and Glu) at the -3 and -2 positions for c-Src.
source: Negatively-charged amino acids (Asp and Glu) are also preferred at these positions, and the negative charge on the carboxymethyl group of CMF at neutral pH may be able to mimic this recognition.
evidence: Inferred from screening data and chemical properties

claim: CMF is depleted at the +3 position for c-Src.
source: The charged carboxymethyl group on CMF is likely to be incompatible with this mode of binding, consistent with depletion of CMF at this site (Figure 7D).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Lys is unfavorable for c-Src at every position around the phospho-acceptor tyrosine.
source: Lys is unfavorable for c-Src at every position around the phospho-acceptor tyrosine.
evidence: Observed in screening data

claim: AcK was not only tolerated, but even favorable at a few positions for c-Src.
source: By contrast, AcK was not only tolerated, but even favorable at a few positions (Figure 7D).
evidence: Observed in screening data shown in Figure 7D

claim: All three kinases (c-Src, Hck, and c-Abl) had very similar position-dependent tolerance for AcK over Lys.
